gaps: All three records need new quantity meanings and units, so all are requires-extension; duplicate search covered the supplied catalog-inventory.json (no biology records) and batches b01-b04.
The 19.2 drift-figure trajectory (p = q = .5 -> .7/.3 -> loss of b) is a stochastic-illustration outcome, not a reusable deterministic relationship, and was considered and deliberately not curated.

Muskellunge weight-length illustration on the Allometry page was considered and rejected: the two printed point pairs (30 in/8 lb, 40 in/18 lb) do not reproduce the printed 3.325 exponent (ratio check gives ~2.6 vs ~2.25), so no defensible reference pair exists without the underlying dataset.
handoff.review_notes: Validation: schema + arithmetic + guard checks to be run with the kit validator; packed ZIP to be re-validated. Source-fidelity review by curator: the PNAS/Matthews power-model equation, slope and R2 were read on the PMC page on 2026-11-01 (Table 1 logc value itself was not reached and is not used); the 19.2 heritability sentence and gene-pool-share sentences were read on the OpenStax page on 2026-11-01. No review corrections were supplied.
handoff.summary: Batch b05: three atomic biology records (island species-area power scaling with the published global plant slope, narrow-sense-agnostic heritability fraction, per-individual gene-pool share) grounded in Matthews et al. PNAS 2026 via PMC and OpenStax Biology 2e section 19.2, each with two references, domain and missing-input rejections, and inverse notes.

assumptions: source assumption: FITTED empirical regularity, not a derived law: the power model 'provides the best general solution' by comparative model fitting, with NatRich slope z = 0.32 at R2 = 66 percent; residual variation is attributed to isolation, island origins and endemism.

source assumption: scope is noncumulative island totals (ISAR: 'the number of species occurring within each of a set of islands as a function of the area of each island'), fitted here for native vascular-plant richness across 1,262 islands; area alone is 'almost never sufficient' and the paper reports no upper asymptote.

source assumption: normalization c is the fitted richness at unit area for the island group (the intercept 'logc (the log-transformed richness of an island of unit area)'); it is an input here, varying by group, not a universal constant.

gaps: Quantity meanings fitted_richness_normalization, island_area and species_richness and the fitted exponent z are not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot; runtime projection omitted.

models.inverse_notes: Island area is recoverable only through the (1/z) power, which needs logarithms/roots outside the scalar profile; no inverse case is tested. The unit-area identity runs both ways: A = 1 gives S = c, and S = c with fixed c implies A = 1. Zero area is excluded by the guard (richness is defined for positive island areas in the ISAR framing).
limitations: A global-average trend, not a per-island predictor: the paper's own data span orders of magnitude around the fit, and extrapolating the all-islands fit underestimates continental richness.
Not applicable to nested species-accumulation curves, which follow different mathematics (paper's distinction i vs ii).
The fitted slope is scale- and context-dependent (within-archipelago ~0.23-0.33, provinces ~0.9); applying z = 0.32 outside the global-native-plant scope needs its own fit.

references.method: Constructed from the published fitted slope: 2^0.32 = e^(0.32 ln 2) = e^0.2218 = 1.2483, so doubling area multiplies fitted richness by ~1.25 at the global NatRich slope; expected 1.248 with 0.001 tolerance.
references.provenance: Value derived independently from the published fitted exponent via the doubling construction.

references.method: Constructed from the published province-scale slope (Rosenzweig, quoted as z = c. 0.9): 2^0.9 = e^0.6238 = 1.8661; materially different case showing the steeper province scaling with the same expression.
references.provenance: Value derived independently from the published province-scale exponent via the doubling construction.

rejection_cases.reason: Richness is defined for positive island areas; a zero-area island has no ISAR richness.
Island area A is required; normalization and slope alone do not determine richness.

relationship.locator: Matthews et al. PNAS 123(8) (2026) via PMC12933073: 'The oldest and simplest models proposed to describe ISARs are i) the power model, S = cAz, (eqn 1)'; fitted 'logS = logc + z logA (eqn 3)' with slope z and intercept logc defined as above; abstract reports NatRich z = 0.32 at R2 = 66 percent.
relationship.translation_notes: Source symbols S (species number), A (area), c, z preserved as local S, A, c, z; juxtaposition transcribed as *. The variable exponent z is a dimensionless fitted slope, so no dimensionful power arises. Dimensional check: fitted normalization (species per area^z) times area^z gives a species count. Fitted-vs-theoretical status explicit in assumptions: z = 0.32 is the reported fit, not a law.

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: the power model S = cA^z (eqn 1) with log form logS = logc + z logA (eqn 3); slope z is the richness-increase rate and logc the richness at unit area; global native-plant fit z = 0.32, R2 = 66 percent over 1,262 islands; within-archipelago z = 0.23-0.33 vs province z = c. 0.9; no upper asymptote supported; area alone almost never sufficient.

assumptions: source assumption: phenotypic variation is partitioned so that a fraction is attributable to genetic differences ('genetic variability') among individuals; the page defines heritability as exactly that fraction.
source assumption: the record is population- and environment-relative: it inherits the page's framing of variation within a population under its environment, not a fixed property of a trait.

gaps: Quantity meanings genetic_variance, phenotypic_variance and heritability are not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot; runtime projection omitted.

models.inverse_notes: Genetic variance is recoverable as VG = h2 * VP. Substitution check: 0.3 * 100 = 30, consistent with the ordinary reference. VP = 0 is excluded (no variation means no fraction); VG = 0 gives h2 = 0 (all variation environmental), which is admissible.
limitations: Population- and environment-specific: the same trait can show different heritability in another population or environment.
The page does not distinguish narrow-sense (additive) from broad-sense heritability; that distinction is outside this record's scope.

references.method: Constructed check: 30 of 100 variance units attributed to genetic differences gives 30/100 = 0.3; verifies encoding, no field value claimed.
references.provenance: Independently constructed arithmetic check; not a published field value.

references.method: Boundary: zero genetic variance gives heritability 0 (all phenotypic variation environmental).
references.provenance: Definitional boundary check with explicit meaning.

rejection_cases.reason: Genetic variance cannot exceed the total phenotypic variance it partitions.
Total phenotypic variance VP is required; genetic variance alone is not a fraction.

relationship.locator: Section 19.2 'Genetic variability': 'Heritability is the fraction of phenotype variation that we can attribute to genetic differences, or genetic variability, among individuals in a population.'
relationship.original_equation: heritability = geneticphenotypic variation fraction (prose definition, no printed symbols)
relationship.translation_notes: Prose definition formalized as a ratio; VG (genetic variance) and VP (phenotypic variance) introduced (the page uses prose, not symbols). Dimensional check: variance over variance gives a dimensionless fraction.

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: heritability is the fraction of phenotype variation attributable to genetic differences (genetic variability) among individuals; higher heritability means more susceptibility to forces acting on heritable variation.

assumptions: source assumption: diploid sexual population in which each individual carries an equal 1/N share of the gene copies at a locus (2 of 2N); the page's '1/10 of the population's gene pool' for 1 of 10 individuals and '1 percent' for 1 of 100.
source assumption: conceptual equal-share illustration of drift susceptibility, not a sampling probability or an observed allele frequency.

gaps: Quantity meanings census_size and gene_pool_share are not in the runtime vocabulary snapshot; runtime projection omitted.

models.inverse_notes: Census size is recoverable as N = 1 / s. Substitution check: 1 / 0.1 = 10, consistent with the drift reference. N = 0 is excluded (an empty population has no gene pool); fractional N has no meaning and the domain is whole individuals.
limitations: Equal-share concept only; real individuals differ in actual allelic content and reproductive contribution.

Illustrates why small populations are drift-susceptible; it is not itself a drift probability or a prediction of allele loss. The figure's .5 -> .7 -> loss trajectory is stochastic illustration and is not formalized here.

references.method: Published illustration: one individual of 10 holds '1/10 of the population's gene pool'; 1/10 = 0.1 exact.
Published illustration: one individual of 100 holds 'only 1 percent of the overall gene pool'; 1/100 = 0.01 exact.

rejection_cases.reason: An empty population has no gene pool to share.
Census size N must be supplied; a gene-pool share cannot be determined from no input.

relationship.locator: Section 19.2 'Genetic Drift': 'If one individual of a population of 10 individuals happens to die ... all of its genes-1/10 of the population's gene pool-will be suddenly lost. In a population of 100, that's only 1 percent of the overall gene pool'.
relationship.original_equation: individual gene-pool share = 1 / N (from the 1-of-10 and 1-of-100 sentences)
relationship.translation_notes: Two printed sentences formalized as the reciprocal of census size; N (census) and s (share) introduced (the page uses prose, not symbols). Dimensional check: pure number over count is treated as a dimensionless share of the whole pool.

sources.evidence: Paraphrase: losing 1 of 10 individuals loses 1/10 of the gene pool, while 1 of 100 is only 1 percent; small populations are therefore more susceptible to genetic drift than large ones.
